title: AI leadership: Practicing what we preach
author: A&O Shearman · Francesca Bennetts · Peter Van Dyck · Alexander Touma

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source reinforces the need for professional governance and legal compliance independently of insurance, adding concrete detail on function-specific controls and fragmented jurisdictional requirements. It does not address coverage wording, policy lines, claims data or insurance pricing.
qs: Other clients need help implementing governance frameworks to set boundaries on how employees can use AI across business functions including engineering, HR, communications, legal, and business, which all have different risk profiles.

“We assist clients with developing and deploying AI products in a manner that complies with regulations, such as obtaining and using data to train generative AI, end-user disclosures, and risk mitigation policies and measures.”  On the commercial side, the firm assists clients by drafting and negotiating agreements related to the development and use of generative AI services.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s account of regulatory divergence, implementation delays and risk-based EU compliance, while materially extending it with practical examples of cross-jurisdictional advice and a business-facing AI Act classification tool. It welcomes simplification as client relief but treats the proposed pause as prospective and does not establish either regulatory effectiveness or independently measured efficiency gains.
qs: “We’re seeing a lot of our clients struggle with how these frameworks all fit together, and how they can comply with all of them at the same time,” notes Peter.

Combining tech and legal expertise, it enables clients to answer a set of questions (such as how the systems work and what purposes they serve) to find out which risk level their systems would be classified as under the EU AI Act.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: A&O Shearman endorses the cluster’s integrated-delivery proposition and adds a concrete firm-level model: multidisciplinary teams build AI solutions for both internal and client use, while lawyers’ everyday deployment experience feeds product refinement. This illustrates organisational capability and workflow integration, although it does not establish measured client outcomes or market-wide value capture.
qs: Through our Markets Innovation Group (MIG), a practice comprising lawyers, developers, and technologists, we continue to innovate by building generative AI solutions used internally and directly by our clients.

We’ve given our people access to the best tools and provided extensive training, while developing and sharing best practices.”  Because our lawyers use generative AI themselves, we can apply their practical experience to inform and refine our products.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s selective-deployment logic and adds a concrete bounded workflow: guided EU AI Act risk classification that combines legal and technical expertise, shifts initial analysis to business users and claims time savings for legal departments. It illustrates task redesign rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, although its promotional account does not establish verification quality or realised organisational value independently.
qs: Combining tech and legal expertise, it enables clients to answer a set of questions (such as how the systems work and what purposes they serve) to find out which risk level their systems would be classified as under the EU AI Act.
Using the tool, a company’s business team can complete the task without needing specialist knowledge, saving time for legal departments.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: A&O Shearman supports the cluster’s proposition that competitive advantage comes from combining legal expertise with hands-on AI deployment, integrated workflows and multidisciplinary capability rather than merely acquiring a strong model. Its account also reinforces the need for sustained adoption, training and product refinement, but offers claims and deployment descriptions rather than quantified evidence of durable competitive superiority.
qs: The breadth and depth of our expertise, combined with the insights generated from building and deploying systems, puts us at the forefront of the marketplace with our AI adoption and advisory capabilities.

Through our Markets Innovation Group (MIG), a practice comprising lawyers, developers, and technologists, we continue to innovate by building generative AI solutions used internally and directly by our clients.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: A&O Shearman supports the cluster’s operating-model framing by describing enterprise-wide adoption built around multidisciplinary development, sustained training, bespoke workflows and feedback from lawyers’ practical use. It also illustrates differentiated delivery architecture linking AI-enabled solutions to advisory capability, but provides no quantified outcomes or evidence on bargaining power and pricing shifts.
qs: Through our Markets Innovation Group (MIG), a practice comprising lawyers, developers, and technologists, we continue to innovate by building generative AI solutions used internally and directly by our clients.

We’ve given our people access to the best tools and provided extensive training, while developing and sharing best practices.”  Because our lawyers use generative AI themselves, we can apply their practical experience to inform and refine our products.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Touma supports the cluster’s emphasis on multidisciplinary implementation by arguing that complex, cross-jurisdictional AI deployments require input from multiple legal practice groups. His additional claim that only large global firms can provide such advice is unsupported in the supplied evidence and does not materially establish the cluster’s broader focus on verification, evaluation or accessible delivery.
qs: “These are sophisticated companies deploying very complex products across many jurisdictions with varying regulatory regimes, which requires the input of many practice groups.

Only large global firms like A&O Shearman can advise on this level of complexity.”  Alexander Touma  Partner  [Read more about our artificial intelligence capabilities](/en/expertise/artificial-intelligence).

kp.k: Internal AI adoption informs advisory work and product development
kp.d: The firm presents AI advisory and building AI-enabled solutions as mutually reinforcing activities: lawyers’ practical use informs products and client advice. It claims to have been the first firm to implement generative AI at enterprise level in 2022. Francesca Bennetts describes three years of embedding tools, training and shared practices; these are firm-reported activities rather than independently measured outcomes.
qs: In 2022, we became the first firm to implement generative AI at an enterprise level.

We have used the last three years to embed the use of generative AI in our lawyers’ day-to-day work. We’ve given our people access to the best tools and provided extensive training, while developing and sharing best practices.
Because our lawyers use generative AI themselves, we can apply their practical experience to inform and refine our products.

kp.k: Multidisciplinary teams turn lawyer expertise into technology products
kp.d: The Markets Innovation Group combines lawyers, developers and technologists to build tools for internal and client use. Bennetts attributes product differentiation to substantial lawyer development time, bespoke prompt engineering and workflows, and incorporating 20–30 years of legal, market and product knowledge. Her claims that tools are tested and workable are not accompanied by performance measurements.
qs: Through our Markets Innovation Group (MIG), a practice comprising lawyers, developers, and technologists, we continue to innovate by building generative AI solutions used internally and directly by our clients.
Where we are unique is that we have invested a significant amount of lawyer time in developing these tools.
We are distilling 20–30 years’ worth of legal, market and product knowledge from our lawyers’ brains to create solutions that deliver the expertise of the firm within a technology tool.

kp.k: Contract tools combine internal deployment with client licensing
kp.d: ContractMatrix, developed with Harvey and Microsoft, is available to all firm lawyers and licensed to clients. The firm reports using it to accelerate contract drafting, review and negotiation. Analyze launched in July 2025 to align reviews with playbooks or policies, while ContractMatrix Vantage extends the offering to analysis across large document portfolios. No quantified time savings are supplied.
qs: Our lawyers are using it to speed up the drafting, reviewing, and negotiating of contracts.
All of our lawyers have access to ContractMatrix, and it is also available as a product for clients to license.
Most recently, MIG developed ContractMatrix Vantage, another lawyer-led tool, which uses generative AI to conduct complex, precise legal analysis across large portfolios of documents.

kp.k: Partner advocacy encourages associate and junior AI engagement
kp.d: Bennetts reports that seeing the tools’ capabilities has converted previous sceptics into advocates who encourage associates and juniors to engage with AI. This is an anecdotal account of adoption dynamics, not evidence of changes to headcount, leverage or promotion.
qs: What’s really exciting is seeing previous sceptics become passionate advocates because they can see what we can do with the tools we have built. Now, they are motivating their associates and juniors to engage proactively with AI.

kp.k: Regulatory change prompts proactive, scalable legal-tool development
kp.d: Regulatory, Finance and MIG teams are developing a ContractMatrix Vantage module for loan transfer reviews at scale in connection with CRD VI, which the document says will enter into force in January 2027. Bennetts describes upfront prototyping and testing based on anticipated client implementation difficulties, rather than a completed deployment with measured results.
qs: Together, our Regulatory, Finance and MIG teams are building a ContractMatrix Vantage module to handle loan transfer reviews at scale.

We’ve spent time upfront thinking about what an AI-enabled solution could look like, building a prototype, and testing it. Now, we’re able to share the results of this investment directly with clients,

kp.k: Regulatory fragmentation generates cross-border advisory demand
kp.d: Peter van Dyck attributes AI advisory and transactional demand to clients’ difficulties complying with disparate regimes. Examples include a multi-jurisdictional governance program, worldwide drug-discovery advice and a financial institution’s global contracting templates and policies. He argues that this work requires both detailed local knowledge and global coordination.
qs: Where our clients struggle is in how to comply with often disparate AI regulatory regimes across the world,
This has led to a flurry of AI advisory and transactional work.
For these types of multi-jurisdictional projects, we need intimate knowledge of various legal regimes, together with an in-depth understanding of the best practices in each of the relevant markets.

kp.k: Self-service classification shifts analysis to client business teams
kp.d: The firm describes a questionnaire-based EU AI Act classifier developed across offices led by Luxembourg. Van Dyck says business teams can classify systems without specialist knowledge, replacing what would normally require hours of manual legal analysis and saving legal departments time. The document provides no accuracy assessment or quantified deployment results.
qs: Normally, he points out, establishing whether a system is prohibited risk, high-risk, or limited risk would take hours of manual analysis by legal teams.
Using the tool, a company’s business team can complete the task without needing specialist knowledge, saving time for legal departments.

kp.k: EU divergence and proposed simplification complicate compliance planning
kp.d: Van Dyck says clients struggle to reconcile overlapping EU frameworks and that the anticipated international diffusion of the AI Act has not materialised, contrasting US deregulation and the UK’s wait-and-see approach. The document reports withdrawal of what it calls the European Liability Directive and describes the November 19, 2025 Digital Omnibus as proposing, rather than implementing, a pause of up to 16 months for high-risk AI provisions and other simplifications. Van Dyck welcomes this as potential compliance relief.
qs: We’re seeing a lot of our clients struggle with how these frameworks all fit together, and how they can comply with all of them at the same time,
So far, we have not yet seen much of the so-called ‘Brussels Effect’,

Most importantly, the Commission published a Digital Omnibus package on November 19, 2025, which—together with several other simplifications—intends to pause the implementation of the AI Act’s provisions on high-risk AI systems for a period of up to 16 months.

kp.k: US federal ambitions coexist with state compliance obligations
kp.d: The document contrasts Biden-era guardrails with Trump executive orders promoting domestic AI expansion. It reports disagreement over federal pre-emption and says the December 2025 executive order does not itself displace state statutes: federal legislation is required, while the administration intends to pursue litigation and agency policy. Touma identifies potentially greater compliance difficulties for smaller, less sophisticated companies, while noting similar fragmentation in privacy and biometrics.
qs: However, the executive order does not itself unilaterally pre-empt state statutes.
For now, AI regulations in the U.S. remain a patchwork of state laws.
This patchwork of regulations may make it harder for smaller and less sophisticated companies to comply. But this was already the case for other legal areas such as data privacy and biometrics.

kp.k: State legislation creates differentiated requirements and changing implementation dates
kp.d: The document reports California’s September 2025 SB 53 requirements for frontier-model transparency, safety and catastrophic-risk mitigation, alongside penalties and whistleblower protections, and October 2025 AB 853 transparency and disclosure expansion. It describes Colorado’s 2024 comprehensive law covering consequential high-risk decisions, including legal services, and its implementation delay from February 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 following an August 2025 special session.
qs: In October 2025, Governor Newsom also signed AB 853 into law, which expands transparency and disclosure requirements for generative AI systems, large online platforms, and capture device manufacturers.

Earlier in 2024, Colorado passed the first comprehensive AI law targeting high-risk systems that make consequential decisions (such as those regarding education, financial services, housing, and legal services).

The law was originally scheduled to take effect on February 1, 2026, but following a special legislative session in August 2025, Colorado delayed implementation of the law until June 30, 2026, to allow further considerations of amendments.

kp.k: AI advice spans product design, commercial contracts and governance
kp.d: Touma describes advising clients of varying sizes on training-data use, disclosures, risk mitigation, AI service agreements and partnerships. Governance work sets boundaries for employee AI use across functions with different risk profiles. A reported matter concerned New York City Local Law 144 and automated decisions by a proposed tool for an in-house employment team. Where precedents are absent, lawyers collaborate with clients to establish practices for systems, policies and terms.
qs: We assist clients with developing and deploying AI products in a manner that complies with regulations, such as obtaining and using data to train generative AI, end-user disclosures, and risk mitigation policies and measures.

Other clients need help implementing governance frameworks to set boundaries on how employees can use AI across business functions including engineering, HR, communications, legal, and business, which all have different risk profiles.

Because there isn’t always a precedent for processes like architecting systems, setting policies, or dictating terms, lawyers are able to work alongside clients to brainstorm and determine best practices.

kp.k: Financial AI agents require multidisciplinary deployment safeguards
kp.d: The firm reports helping a financial institution develop agents intended to provide financial advice and services. Planned work involves technology transactions, financial services, privacy and cybersecurity lawyers across jurisdictions, with safeguards limiting outputs to legally permissible information and educating customers about risks. Touma argues that only large global firms can handle this complexity; this is his competitive-positioning claim, not a demonstrated market finding.
qs: We are also helping a large financial institution develop AI agents, which will provide financial advice and services.
This includes ensuring that the AI technology does not provide output that goes beyond the type of information that is permitted under applicable law.
Only large global firms like A&O Shearman can advise on this level of complexity.

kp.k: Training-data risks expand diligence and ongoing legal advice
kp.d: Touma describes AI acquisition diligence examining development practices, training-data sources, policies and contracts, alongside advice to technology companies on sourcing data directly and through partners across jurisdictions. Despite substantial litigation, including training-data IP claims, he observes that the race to develop and deploy AI appears to increase sector companies’ tolerance for risk. This is a practitioner observation, not a quantified finding.
qs: Alex has also worked on M&A transactions assisting clients on acquiring AI technology, with due diligence covering areas such as the target’s development practices including the source of data used to train AI technology, and the policies and contracts governing it.

However, Alex observes that despite significant volume of litigation around AI technology (including IP infringement risks arising from the use of training data), sector companies appear to have a higher tolerance for risk given the race to develop and deploy the technology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source presents AI as changing both the delivery of legal work and demand for legal advice, with practical AI development positioned as a competitive advantage.
pts.d: A&O Shearman claims that building and using AI tools improves its advisory capabilities and enables it to package legal expertise into products used by lawyers and licensed by clients. Francesca Bennetts attributes better-tailored products to substantial lawyer involvement, technical expertise and practical feedback. The firm says ContractMatrix speeds contract drafting, review and negotiation; Analyze streamlines review against playbooks or policy requirements; and ContractMatrix Vantage performs complex analysis across document portfolios. Bennetts describes a prototype module intended to handle loan transfer reviews at scale for CRD VI implementation. Peter van Dyck describes a self-service EU AI Act classifier that shifts a task ordinarily requiring hours of legal analysis to business teams without specialist knowledge. Separately, van Dyck and Alexander Touma describe AI deployment and fragmented regulation as generating advisory, contracting, governance, transactional and due-diligence work. Touma claims that complex global deployments require multiple practice groups and that only large global firms can advise at that level of complexity. He also observes that technology companies appear more tolerant of litigation risk because of competition to develop and deploy AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on the firm's reported implementation experience, partner testimony, product descriptions and anonymised client matters.
pts.d: The firm reports enterprise-level generative AI implementation in 2022, three years of embedding use, extensive training, lawyer-led research and development, and prototype testing. Bennetts describes incorporating 20–30 years of lawyers' accumulated knowledge into tools and reports sceptics becoming advocates. These are experience-based accounts rather than measured productivity or quality findings: the source supplies no comparative benchmarks, error rates, quantified savings or detailed testing results. The classifier's time-saving claim likewise has no accompanying measured study. Examples supporting demand for advice include a multi-jurisdictional governance programme, worldwide drug-discovery advice, financial-institution contracting policies, an in-house employment AI tool, financial-services AI agents, and AI-related M&A due diligence. Touma's exclusivity claim for large global firms is a partner's market-positioning assertion, not a comparative market finding. The firm also invokes Financial Times recognition as contextual authority for its innovation credentials.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern current practice in the 2025 account; future-oriented claims concern regulatory implementation and tools still being developed.
pts.d: The firm dates enterprise adoption to 2022 and describes the following three years as a period of embedding AI use. Analyze launched in July 2025; Vantage is described as the most recent development. The CRD VI loan-transfer module remains a prototype under development, aimed at rules the source says enter into force in January 2027, rather than a completed deployment with demonstrated outcomes. Product advantages are linked to lawyer-led design, testing, training and tailoring to client requirements. Demand for global advice is conditioned on regulatory divergence, deployment complexity and sector-specific constraints. Van Dyck describes the November 19, 2025 Digital Omnibus proposal as potentially providing regulatory breathing room, including an intended pause of up to 16 months for high-risk AI provisions; the source presents these as proposed changes, not completed implementation. Touma describes the US state-law patchwork as persisting despite the December 2025 federal executive order, and records Colorado's implementation delay to June 30, 2026. The article does not predict a date for lawyer displacement or profession-wide staffing change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are firm lawyers and multidisciplinary development teams, corporate legal and business teams, AI developers and deployers, and global legal-service providers.
pts.d: Firm lawyers gain tools for contract work and portfolio analysis while contributing expertise to product development; Bennetts reports senior advocates encouraging associates and juniors to engage with AI. MIG combines lawyers, developers and technologists. Corporate clients can license firm-developed tools, while business teams can use the classifier to reduce demands on legal departments. Corporate buyers seek advice across engineering, HR, communications, legal and other business functions. Examples span financial institutions, life sciences companies, Silicon Valley technology businesses and an in-house employment team. Touma says smaller and less sophisticated companies may have greater difficulty complying with fragmented rules, while complex multinational clients require cross-practice, global advice. The source positions large global firms as beneficiaries of this complexity but offers no specific staffing, fee, employment or access-to-justice forecast.
